I hope you can overcome it too! Texture was (and still is) one of my biggest issues when it comes to food and trying to like new things. Along with a big aversion in my personality to trying new things without 'testing the waters' in some regard first. I find a few things helped with the textural thing, so I'll share them.

Firstly: make it look appetising to you. We eat with our eyes, so if something is presented well, you will be more inclined to try it than if it looks like someone just threw up on the plate.

Secondly: try new things with familiar things, or try to hide the texture with another more pleasant texture until you get more used to it. Or just have something in small amounts.

Thirdly: Get used to the idea that your aversion is in your head. Nowadays when I'm faced with something new, or something that I had established as a kid that I didn't like without even trying it, I say things to myself like 'it's not going to kill me if I eat this."

Lastly: Our aversions mostly come through association from other things we've experienced. So, for example, if you had a bad experience with one type of veggie, like say broccoli, your brain may begin to associate green food, anything that looks like broccoli, or veggies in general with that negative experience. So then when you encounter say silverbeet which is a green leafy vegetable, your brain may unconsciously assume 'green = gross, therefore I won't like it' without even trying it. This further reinforces the idea, even without the experience to go with it. But you can also use this 'by association' mechanism to ease yourself into trying new things as well. For example, go with a vegetable you know you like, and pair it with something else you haven't tried but that is similar and create a positive experience reinforced by something you already know. Gradually, you'll be able to tackle things you haven't liked in the past.

These are the little things that have worked for me, but it's important to experiment and find out what works for you. You're lucky that hopefully you'll be able to get some nice home grown veggies yum! Learning to properly cook things to the way that you like them is important as well, because everyone has different palettes. Your tastes definitely tend to shift as you get older too. Trying to cut out as much sugar and processed food will also develop your sense of taste better. Also, accept that there are things that you may never like, and if you have a bad experience leave it alone and come back to it at a later date when the memory has faded a bit. It might be different the second go around :) Hope I've been able to give you a place to start at least :)
